principalQuestion: How did hub retain the idea of a center while becoming available to describe places, routes, institutions, networks, and digital services?

exclusions.rule: Successful non-background, unhyphenated two-token queries; raw-note ambiguous, sparse, and mechanical-adjacent rows excluded.

evidence.summary: Webster's 1828 dictionary entry treats hub/hob as the nave of a wheel and the timber part receiving the spokes.
evidence.sourceTitle: An American Dictionary of the English Language
evidence.caveat: Historical dictionary evidence, not a first-use quotation or non-dictionary corpus example.

evidence.summary: Holmes uses hub metaphorically for Boston's central self-conception.
evidence.caveat: Project Gutenberg text confirms the passage; first-edition page verification would further strengthen publication details.

evidence.summary: Cycling periodical context uses wheel hub mechanically in relation to bicycle equipment.
evidence.caveat: OCR heading appears partly garbled around 'Front'; image verification is recommended before publication.

evidence.summary: First-pass snippet for railway hub in transport and logistics node.
evidence.sourceTitle: Image 8 of The Washington daily news (Washington, D.C.), December 3, 1943
evidence.caveat: Imported from first-pass snippets; OCR/readability and source image should be checked before final use.

evidence.summary: Defines hub-and-spoke as an air-traffic routing system and lists first known use as 1980.
evidence.caveat: Dictionary claim for a specific transport-system adjective; no quotation visible in the public entry.

figureContracts.title: One word, six kinds of center
figureContracts.researchQuestion: When do the selected semantic families become visible?
filters: exclude raw-note ambiguous, sparse, and mechanical-adjacent rows
figureContracts.formula: unweighted twenty-year arithmetic mean; visible at >= 0.002 per million
figureContracts.unit: period and percent of eligible family phrases
figureContracts.missingnessPolicy: failed queries are excluded, never displayed as zero
figureContracts.caveat: proxy visibility is not semantic population prevalence

figureContracts.title: The original line falls; the others rise around it
figureContracts.researchQuestion: How do selected family means change across the twentieth century?
figureContracts.missingnessPolicy: all retained annual rows must be present; failure blocks the phrase

figureContracts.title: More ways to be a center
figureContracts.researchQuestion: How broadly is the same phrase inventory visible in three comparison periods?
figureContracts.denominator: 39 eligible phrases in every displayed period
figureContracts.missingnessPolicy: failed and excluded queries do not enter the fixed denominator
figureContracts.caveat: not an estimate of all English hub usage

figureContracts.title: Persistence and change
figureContracts.researchQuestion: Which selected phrases are durable, recent, rising, or falling?
figureContracts.denominator: six periods for persistence; phrase-specific means for change
figureContracts.formula: x = visible period count; y = 2000–2019 mean − 1980–1999 mean
figureContracts.missingnessPolicy: below threshold remains observed below-threshold, not missing
figureContracts.caveat: recent growth can be large from a very small base

figureContracts.title: Evidence anchors
figureContracts.researchQuestion: What dated evidence supports key transitions?
figureContracts.missingnessPolicy: dictionary claim remains distinct from direct text
figureContracts.caveat: the dictionary records establish availability, not first use

figureContracts.title: Phrase trajectories
figureContracts.researchQuestion: How do representative phrases carry the larger movement?
filters: six pre-registered representative phrases from the production inventory
visualChannelMapping: y = phrase mean on a shared scale
figureContracts.missingnessPolicy: all six selected phrases have complete annual rows
figureContracts.caveat: examples illustrate the selected inventory and are not exhaustive
